active_themes.label: Gulf Oil Slowly Returns
active_themes.summary: Brent fell 8.67% to $94.62 and WTI 8.29% to $88.12, taking crude well below the $100 line on bets that politics will restrain the war. No deal is signed and ships are still catching fire near Hormuz, so the drop rests on expectations. The open question is whether Brent holds under $100 without physical proof that shipping is safer.

active_themes.label: Global Borrowing Costs Climb
active_themes.summary: The 10-year yield fell 0.06 points to 4.89% and the 30-year fell 0.04 points to 5.28%, the first relief in a while, and it came with the oil drop. Both remain close to levels that have strained borrowers, with inflation at 3.7%. The open question is whether the 10-year can fall toward 4.75% or oil's slide fades and yields turn back toward 5.00%.

active_themes.label: Iran War Resumption Risk
active_themes.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says two tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, and oil still fell sharply. Markets are treating the diplomatic and political track as stronger than the incidents. The open question is whether these fires become a pattern of sustained attacks on shipping, which would erase today's oil drop.

active_themes.label: AI Spending Backlash
active_themes.summary: The Nasdaq rose 1.44% to 25,737, extending its bounce, but it is still short of the 26,713 recovery line. Voters in several places backed candidates who favor data-center moratoriums, adding a political obstacle to AI building. The open question is whether the Nasdaq reclaims 26,713 or whether doubts about AI spending return once the oil relief fades.

active_themes.label: Democratic Sweep Reaction
active_themes.summary: Democrats swept the midterms, and markets are now reading the result as a brake on tariffs, the war and pressure on the Fed, with the S&P 500 up 1.58%, the dollar down 0.35% and yields lower. A Democratic Senate also has a say over Fed board appointments. The open question is whether the result changes the inflation and deficit picture, which bond buyers care about most.

active_themes.label: Fed Eyes Another Hike
active_themes.summary: The Fed held rates after September's hike, with third-quarter growth at 3.4% and inflation at 3.7%, leaving little case to ease. An 8% oil drop eases the inflation pressure behind a hike, but one session does not change the trend. The open question is whether oil stays low enough to take a December hike off the table.

Fear would be rising from a moderate level to a stress level, a sign that selling has become forced rather than selective.
Small caps breaking lower would show the damage has moved beyond big tech into the broader economy.
Bond buyers finally believe cheaper oil will last, which would be the first real sign of relief on borrowing costs.
The AI-spending doubt is deepening beyond a two-day reaction and big tech is heading for a larger correction.
The longest borrowing costs would be pushing meaningfully higher, deepening the strain on mortgages, stocks and company borrowing.
That would mark a full repair of the AI selloff and show today's bounce was the start of a recovery, not a pause.

The market has given back almost all of today's 3% jump, which would say the rally was a one-day reaction to oil and the election.
